best_for: Windows users who open archives of every kind, from RAR and ISO to VHDX, and want a free tool they can also install on work machines without a license.
description:
7-Zip is a file archiver written and maintained by Igor Pavlov. He also publishes the LZMA SDK, the compression code that 7-Zip's own 7z format is built on.

Once installed, 7-Zip adds itself to the Windows right-click menu, so you can pack or unpack files without opening a program first. It also has its own file manager, and a command-line version you can call from scripts. You can turn a 7z archive into a self-extracting file that opens on a PC without 7-Zip installed. The interface comes in 87 languages, and there is a plugin for the FAR Manager file manager.

points.title: Free at work too
points.text: 7-Zip costs nothing and needs no registration, including in companies. Most of the code is LGPL, some parts are BSD, and the RAR decoder carries the unRAR restriction.

points.title: Opens far more than it makes
points.text: It creates 7z, ZIP, GZIP, BZIP2, XZ, TAR and WIM. It can only extract the long tail, such as RAR, ISO, DMG, CAB, MSI, VHDX and VMDK, so you cannot make a RAR file with it.

points.title: Password protection that holds up
points.text: The 7z format uses AES-256, with the key derived from your password through many rounds of SHA-256. That makes guessing a password slow for an attacker.

points.title: Smaller files, by its own measure
points.text: The project says its ZIP and GZIP output is 2 to 10 percent smaller than PKZip and WinZip produce. The 7z format, built on LZMA and LZMA2, aims for a higher ratio still.

points.title: The graphical app is Windows only
points.text: Linux and Mac get console builds only, as .tar.xz downloads from the project site. This listing covers Windows, where the installers are x86, x64, Arm and Arm64 .exe files plus x86 and x64 MSI packages.

points.title: Silent installs and old systems
points.text: The .exe takes `/S` and the MSI takes `/q` for unattended installs, and all of them install for the whole machine. The project lists support back to Windows 2000 and XP.

points.title: Use 64-bit for big dictionaries
points.text: The FAQ notes that 32-bit Windows gives each program about 2 GB of address space, so very large compression dictionaries can fail there. The Windows listing keeps 24 versions.
